title: Loans, advances and studio time for musicians
summary: He loaned money to musicians, was falsely accused by one he wired money to, and let artists record on credit owed only if the record was leased.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Personally, you mean? Yes. I know one guy in this town, still playing, who called me from Baltimore. The show went bust. And I need money to get home.

And I wired him the money to get home. And that same guy, maybe three years later, in a conversation with a true friend of mine, said I robbed him. Oh, sure. Okay. And that's painful, you know? Because I don't want anybody to give me any great praise, but don't lie about me.
So when you made these loans, it wasn't like whatever it was? I mean, it wasn't...

No, because I was doing that long before I ever was making any money, before I ever started a record company. In other words, you know, once I started a record company, I was giving people advances. And there, you know, and again, I don't want to pat myself on the back, but I owned a recording studio. And I put people into the studio to do the recordings that they were going to later lease to me. If they wanted to, they could lease them to anybody they wanted. I didn't say, if you go into the studio, you've got to give it to me, because I didn't do that. But if they leased it with me, they owed me for the recording time, if they got a lease. If they didn't get a lease with me or anybody else, they didn't owe me for the recording time. You know? And I did a ton of that. Right. It was like we were in it together. You know? I'm one of the guys in the band, and I've got the studio, so we're going to use my studio. You know?
I did a lot of that. Which some guys remember and some forgot.
